1:
Who the angel of Ephesus was Clarke and Ellicott both name; Henry alone refuses. Clarke takes the word for the messenger sent by God to preside over the church, answering to the synagogue officer who read, prayed and taught, and thinks the angel most probably Timothy, who presided before John took up residence there. Ellicott makes it depend on the date of the book: on the earlier date, the reign of Nero or of Galba, the angel is no other than Timothy, and coincidences favour it, since labour and endurance are what Paul acknowledges in him, and there is a latent tone of anxiety in the letters to him, a nature emotional even to tears, ascetic and devout, yet lacking energy. Henry will not have it: one of so excellent a spirit, who cared naturally for the state of souls, could hardly have grown remiss enough to deserve these rebukes.

Whether the letters mean more than they say Clarke settles by an advertisement. He perceives no metaphorical or allegorical meaning in these epistles; he considers the churches real, their spiritual state literally pointed out; he takes the angel for the pastor; and what is spoken to the angel is spoken to the whole church, so that it describes not the pastor's state but the people's under his care. Gill reads the same verse the other way: Ephesus is named first not only as largest and nearest Patmos, but especially because it represented the church in the apostolic age, so that this letter contains the things which are; and he finds in the name a word signifying desire, expressive of that pure church's first fervent love. Bede reads the name too, to another end: Ephesus is interpreted a great fall as well as my will in it, and part of this church he blames and part praises according to the name.

The two titles they weigh for what they promise. Robertson notes that the participle rendered holdeth is stronger than the having of the first chapter, and that walketh alludes to the same vision; the demonstrative rendered these things stands seven times here, once heading each message, and only once elsewhere in the New Testament. Henry takes the first title as protection, the ministers being under Christ's special care: it is the honour of God that he knows the number of the stars and calls them by their names, binds the sweet influences of Pleiades and looses the bands of Orion. Wesley takes it as power and favour together, that they may shine as stars by purity of doctrine and holiness of life, reading the walking by the promise to be with them to the end; he suspects besides an allusion to the priests dressing the lamps, to keep them always burning before the Lord. Bede makes the walking a search of all hearts and reins.

What Ephesus was Robertson sets out. On the Cayster near the sea, foremost city of Asia Minor and temple-keeper of Artemis, home of the magic arts and mystery cults, the place of Paul's three years and John's old age; a free city at the end of the great road from the Euphrates, sixty miles from Patmos, so the messenger reached it first. Its port was shifting sand from the silting of the river's mouth, which is why Ramsay calls it the City of Change. Gill adds that the church seems founded by Paul, who stayed two years till all Asia heard the word. Victorinus paraphrases the opening: I know that thou sufferest and workest, I see that thou art patient, think not that I am staying long from thee; and of the fall he observes that he who falls, falls from a height, which is why the Lord said whence. Barnes notes that each of the four letters opens with an attribute from the first chapter, chosen perhaps for its propriety to that church.
2:
What the knowing amounts to they press hard. Robertson prefers Swete's account of the verb, that it emphasises the absolute clearness of a mental vision which photographs all the facts of life as they pass, adding that where the other verb stands the universal knowledge passes into the field of special observation. Barnes draws the doctrinal consequence: since much that these letters name belongs to the heart, the speaker must have intimate acquaintance with the heart of man, and no one can have that who is not Divine. Ellicott adds the two directions in which it cuts: the veneer of a formal faith might impose on the world but would not escape those flame-like eyes, and he knows and lovingly accepts the unmarked and unrequited acts of true love. Wesley makes it personal: a weighty word, how dreadful it will one day sound to the wicked and how sweet to the righteous, and happy is he who conceives less good of himself than Christ knows of him.

Clarke takes the order of the praise and the blame to be itself instructive. Whatever is praiseworthy in these Churches is mentioned first, which intimates that God is more intent on finding out the good than the evil, and that those who would reform the fallen should take occasion from the good which yet remains to encourage them. At the next verse he notices the reverse: the same things are repeated in inverted order, the reason of which does not appear, though perhaps it was meant to show that no good they had done and no evil they had suffered was forgotten before God. Wesley sees the same shape, three particulars named after the general term and then described more largely in reverse. Gill notes what is absent, that no evil works are charged at all, and nothing is complained of in this church but an abatement of the fervour of her first love.

The third verse needs mending, Ellicott says, to match the best manuscripts: it should stand, and hast patience, and didst bear for my name's sake, and didst not weary, the last word recurring to the word for toil in the verse before. They had toiled on to very weariness, he says, without wearying of their toil, just as they could not bear the evil and yet had borne reproaches for Christ's sake; and he quotes Vaughan: here is toil, patience, abhorrence of evil, discernment, again patience, endurance, unwearied exertion; what can be wanting? Robertson makes the same point from the perfect tense and adds Moffatt's phrase, that they were tired in loyalty and not of it, the church able to bear anything but impostors in her membership. Gill reads the bearing as burdens rather than men, with the Ethiopic, and notes that the Arabic has instead, thou hast borne me.

What is wanting Ellicott will not let the translation soften. Better, he says, I have against thee that thou didst let go; this is the fault, and it is no trifle that is blamed, as the word somewhat, which is not in the original, might be taken to imply, since the decay of love is the decay of that without which all other graces are nothing, all religion being summed up in one word: God asks it, we cannot give more, he cannot take less. Great as it is, he adds, it is the fault which love alone would have detected, and he asks whether any can rebuke more touchingly than by beginning, thou no longer lovest me enough. Robertson calls the verb a definite and sad departure, finding the cause in the controversies with the Nicolaitans, since they remained orthodox and became unloving. Clarke and Wesley insist some love remained, or they could not have acted as they did; Wesley turns it on the reader, asking whether he has kept his own.
5:
The remedy Wesley reduces to three steps, since none can recover the first love but by remembering, repenting and doing the first works; and he ranges the seven letters by that test, two churches in a mixed state, two greatly corrupted, all four exhorted to repent, and two flourishing and exhorted only to steadfastness. Robertson keeps the tenses in view: the perfect marks a settled state, so the fallen must look up from the valley to the cliff where pure love is and whence they came down, while the aorists are urgent, an instant change of attitude and a doing at once, before it is too late. Clarke fills in what is to be remembered: the joy felt at the remission of sins, the zeal for God's glory, the willing obedient spirit, the cheerful self-denial, the fervour in private prayer, the detachment from the world; or else, since the Greek verb is often so used by the best writers, simply what a loss has been sustained.

Gill enters a qualification the others do not: believers cannot totally and finally fall from the grace they have received, though they may fall into sin and from a degree of grace and its exercise, as these first pure churches did; the call to remember is meant to bring them to a sense of their present state and quicken their desire to be restored. Ellicott meanwhile finds the verse pressed into a dispute about the date of the whole book. It is argued that the decay described here proves the later reign, since such a fall might occur in thirty years but hardly in the ten at most between Paul's visit and Nero; he answers that greater changes have passed over communities in equally short periods, nations having been seen to pass from imperialism to republicanism, and from the fever-heat of radicalism to the lethargy of conservatism, in less time.

Who the Nicolaitans were nobody can establish, and Gill defends the man they are named for. They are so called, some think, from Nicolas of Antioch, one of the seven deacons; yet of Nicolas himself it is said that he lived with his own lawful wife and no other, that his daughters continued virgins and his son incorrupt, and that these men only shrouded themselves under his name. Clarke takes them for Gnostics who taught the community of wives, held fornication indifferent and meats offered to idols lawful, and mixed pagan rites with Christian ceremonies. Ellicott calls them the Antinomians of the Asiatic Church, life and conduct little thought of and the professed faith everything, and reports the alternative that the name is purely symbolical, destroyer of the people, no more than the Greek of Balaam. Robertson notes only that a sect of the name existed in the second century, though its descent from the deacon is not certain.

Barnes is the most cautious, holding that from these two passages nothing can now be inferred about the party's doctrines or practices, unless they held what Balaam taught. Of the hatred Robertson borrows Trench's remark, that ancient Greek had words for hatred of evil and for a hater of evil which occur nowhere in the New Testament yet describe this angel exactly. The closing summons Ellicott traces as an echo from the Gospels recurring in all seven letters, before the promise in the first three and after it in the last four, and observes that the hardened heart is the precursor of the deaf ear, spiritual truth needing a spiritual organ, quoting Coleridge that such truths are heard only when the soul seeks to hear, when all is hushed and the heart listens. Robertson adds Swete's word that the Spirit of Christ in the prophet is the interpreter of Christ's voice, and Wesley counts twelve promises across the seven letters, an extract of all the promises of God.
8:
Who the angel of Smyrna was Clarke and Gill both answer with the same name. Clarke says it was probably the famous Polycarp, who was at last burnt alive there about the middle of the second century, and notes that the ancient account of his martyrdom, translated by Cave, reports the Jews as particularly active in it and as bringing the faggots themselves, so that such persons must indeed have been of the synagogue of Satan. Gill adds that Irenaeus, who knew him, says the apostles appointed him bishop there, that the great amphitheatre in which he died was still to be seen and his sepulchre yet preserved, and repeats from the letter of the church itself that three days before his death Polycarp dreamed his pillow was on fire and told those about him what it meant. Robertson notes only that the hostile Jews of the city later took part in that martyrdom.

What kind of city it was they describe in three registers. Ellicott gives commercial figures, the modern Ismir with a population about a hundred and fifty thousand and exports of over a million and three-quarter pounds in one recent year, half of it with England; it has always been reckoned one of the most beautiful cities in Asia, and lies a little north of Ephesus, next to it, as Trench says, in natural order and also in spiritual. Henry calls it a place well known to our merchants, a city of great trade and wealth, and perhaps the only one of the seven still known by the same name, though no longer distinguished for its Christian church. Robertson adds the fact that mattered, a seat of emperor-worship with a temple to Tiberius, and reports Ramsay's name for it, the City of Life, Christianity having held on there better than in any city of Asia.

The poverty they turn into the letter's hinge. Barnes observes that this church alone is called poor, the fact being specified of no other, and that no reason at all is suggested. Robertson sets it against the opposite case and gets his antithesis, that this is a rich poor church and Laodicea a poor rich one, guessing that Jews and pagans may have pillaged what property they had. Wesley makes the contrast a rebuke to the world's estimate: a poor prerogative in the eyes of men, since Philadelphia likewise had but a little strength, and yet these two were the most honourable of all in the eyes of the Lord. Clarke supposes them stripped of their possessions for their attachment to the Gospel, and rich instead in faith; Henry finds in the title, the first and the last, who was dead and is alive, the exact comfort a church about to die needed.

How long the ten days last they will not agree. Clarke takes the days of this book for prophetic days, each answering to a year, so that ten years are meant; Wesley reads them at face value and suspects they began on the very day the Revelation was read at Smyrna, or very soon after. Ellicott turns to the two agents, noting that the Greek Old Testament gives the name devil to Satan as the accuser, and that what the adversary meant as a temptation from allegiance would in effect leave the enduring tested. Robertson points to the writer's own case, John being in exile as he wrote, having often been imprisoned with Peter, while James and Paul and Peter had all suffered martyrdom. Of the promised exemption Ellicott says the phrase second death is new in Bible language, familiar to Jews through the Chaldee paraphrase, and that the later chapters exclude any cessation of conscious existence; Robertson says flatly that it is not annihilation, and Barnes that death here does not mean the soul will cease to be.
12:
What Pergamos was they mark off from the two before it. Ellicott says that, unlike Ephesus and Smyrna, it was no commercial city, its importance owing to other causes: a cone-shaped hill rose from the plain by the Caicus, was held sacred, and being a natural fortress served as keep and treasury for the wealth of local chieftains; its greatness dated from Eumenes, given a large territory by the Romans, who fixed it as his royal residence, raising a splendid place rich in public buildings, temples and galleries, with a library that rivalled Alexandria's. Robertson adds the numbers and the by-product: two hundred thousand volumes second only to Alexandria, Pliny's judgment that it was the most illustrious city of Asia, Ramsay's name for it as the city of authority, and the fact that parchment takes its name from the place. Henry declines to settle whether it rose from the ruins of old Troy.

Why the throne of Satan should stand in this city Ellicott admits he cannot say. The word is throne rather than seat, and the pre-eminence in evil is hard to account for; some leave it unsolved, saying that without any historical notice it must remain one of the riddles of these epistles, while Plumptre appeals to the character of the city, its worship and customs, and the persecutions met there. Robertson accumulates what can be pointed to: Satan had there the seat of power of a king or judge; the symbol of Asklepios was the serpent, as it is of Satan; a throne-altar to Zeus was cut on the acropolis rock, which Swete calls the symbol of rampant paganism; and the new Caesar-worship, with the recent martyrdom of Antipas, made the place a very throne indeed. Wesley says only that Pergamos was above measure given to idolatry, so Satan had full residence there; Clarke reports the Jewish maxim that Satan dwelt where the law of God was unstudied but had to leave wherever a synagogue or academy stood.

The two-edged sword Clarke and Barnes take differently. Clarke expounds it as the sword of the Spirit which cuts every way, piercing between joints and marrow, dividing soul from spirit, dissecting the whole mind and exhibiting a regular anatomy of the soul; it not only reproves sin but slays the ungodly, and Jesus holds it two-edged because he is at once Saviour of sinners and Judge of quick and dead. Barnes is concerned rather with what John saw, and reports Stuart's suggestion that when the Saviour uttered words the breath accompanying them took, to the seer's eye, the form of a fiery two-edged sword; he thinks it likelier that the words took no form at all, and that John means only to represent them as if they were a sword. Wesley reduces the figure to its use here, the sword that cuts off the impenitent.

Ellicott will not let the word few soften the charge, and finds the sting in a repetition. The ground of rebuke is no trifle, since the little leaven might leaven the whole lump, and those brave unto death in persecution proved less proof against seduction; and the church is said to tolerate men holding Balaam's teaching by the very word used two verses earlier in its commendation, thou holdest fast my name. Barnes sharpens the contrast with the first letter, where the same sect was hated and here is harboured. Robertson makes the irony plainer: a party that resisted emperor-worship to the death in Antipas was caught by the insidious wiles Ephesus withstood, Balaam standing, in Charles's phrase, as the prototype of all corrupt teachers. Wesley says they ought to have been cast out of the flock at once, and notes the text has sons of Israel rather than children, set against the daughters of Moab. Gill reads it all of a church still within a corrupt communion it had begun to remonstrate against.
15:
Whether the Balaamites and Nicolaitans are one party they cannot settle. Barnes puts the alternative plainly: if one class is meant, and the Nicolaitans held Balaam's doctrine, we know what their teaching was; if two, we have no means of knowing what was peculiar to the second; and he judges it more natural that they taught the same thing. Ellicott finds opinions divided and prefers to take the wilderness temptation as an illustration of the Pergamene one rather than an identification, since both lead in the same Antinomian direction, a tendency early seen and, he adds, not extinct now. Robertson makes the adverb decide it: they followed Balaam in refusing the Jerusalem conference's decision about idolatry and fornication, and so encouraged a return to pagan laxity; and he dismisses as wrong the notion that they were Pauline Christians. Gill sees in them the later doctrines of Rome, which forbade marriage to the priesthood.

Whom the threat falls on Wesley and Barnes divide differently. Barnes says the coming is against the church for tolerating them, but aimed principally at the offenders, since the church excites displeasure by retaining them while it has power to save them; a church always suffers when it has offenders in its bosom. Wesley reads the clauses as addressed to different parties, so the angel will not wholly escape when the rest are punished, and adds that the fighting is not with the Nicolaitans, mentioned only by the by, but with Balaam's followers, whom he traces into Numbers: Balaam was first withstood by the angel of the Lord with his sword drawn, and afterwards slain with the sword. Robertson quotes Renan's phrase for the clause, an eternal roll of thunder from the throne, and Swete's, that the glorified Christ is in this book a Warrior fighting with the sharp sword of the word; how soon quickly means, he says, we do not know, but the threat is real.

Who hid the manna they answer differently. Clarke reports the constant Jewish tradition that the ark, the tables of stone, Aaron's rod, the anointing oil and the pot of manna were hidden by King Josiah when Jerusalem fell, and shall all be restored in the days of the Messiah; the manna was hidden, and Christ promises it to the conqueror, since Jesus is himself ark, oil, rod, testimony and manna, and he who partakes of his grace has all those things in their spiritual perfection. Robertson gives the office to Jeremiah instead, believed to have hidden the ark before the city fell, where it would not be found till Israel was restored, citing Second Maccabees. Ellicott calls this allusion the obvious one: Israel ate manna in the wilderness and died, while the Father gives the true bread from heaven that a man may eat and not die, and live even though, like Antipas, he die.

The white stone Clarke will not reduce to one thing, offering three. It may be the pebble by which ancient judges gave their suffrages, white absolving and black condemning, so that pardon and its evidence are meant; or the stone given to victors in the public games, inscribed with the name, entitling them for life to maintenance at the public charge; or a Roman tally, of which the sort used at table answered exactly to our cards of invitation to a feast, while the sort exchanged between guest-friends was broken in two and the halves compared to prove the bearer. Wesley takes the first and third together, since the ancients gave their votes by small stones and sometimes wrote on small smooth ones, so here may be an allusion to both; and he compares the new name to the Israel that Jacob gained after his victory. Ellicott grants that not all the allusions are easy, and would read the promise, a new name graven, which no man knoweth but he who receiveth it.
18:
Why the speaker names himself here Barnes takes as deliberate. This is the first time the name is given at all, every other letter opening with an attribute only; perhaps the severity of the rebuke to come required a more impressive reference to authority, so that he is introduced as the Son of God rather than by the title he gave himself on earth, which would have suggested only his humanity. Wesley presses the same contrast, see how great he is who appeared like a son of man. Ellicott looks at the city: Thyatira was a Macedonian colony founded by Alexander after Persia fell, whose colonists introduced the worship of Apollo as Sun-god, so some have thought the eyes of flame were chosen in allusion to that worship under the form of a dazzlingly ornamented image. Robertson notes that Apollo was chief deity there and emperor-worship absent, and reports Ramsay's name for the place, Weakness Made Strong. Henry sets the city between Mysia and Lydia and makes it the home of Lydia the purple-seller who heard Paul at Philippi; Gill reports from Epiphanius that some once denied there was any church at Thyatira at all.

The praise here runs longer than anywhere else, and Robertson counts it. Four graces are named, each with its own article, a longer list than Ephesus received, love standing first in true Johannine fashion; more praise, he observes, is given where blame follows than where no fault is found at all. Ellicott arranges them in two pairs, charity and service being the outward ministrations that manifest the inner principle of love, while patience is the token of faith; and he reads the last clause, thy last works more than the first. Clarke notes that he puts faith before service by the consent of the best manuscripts. Wesley sets the two churches side by side as mixed characters of opposite kinds, one unable to bear the wicked yet fallen from its first love, the other keeping its love yet bearing the wicked.

Whether the text reads that woman or thy wife divides them, and the consequence is why. Clarke reports that many excellent manuscripts and almost all the ancient versions have thy wife Jezebel, a reading which he says intimates, indeed asserts, that she was the bishop's wife, so his criminality in suffering her was the greater. Wesley records the same tradition, that many of the ancients made her the pastor's own wife. Ellicott reports the variant and leaves open whether the influence was in the angel's household. Robertson rejects it outright, and by the very consequence the others accept: some manuscripts have the possessive, which Ramsay renders thy woman, but the best copies rightly omit it, since otherwise she is the pastor's wife. He takes the name as symbolic of some prominent woman in the church, after the queen guilty of whoredom and witchcraft who sought to drive God's worship out of Israel.

Who Jezebel was Barnes and Clarke agree cannot be recovered. Barnes says it is by no means probable this was her real name, but that it was given as expressive of her character; Clarke says that although we do not know who she was, we may take it for granted she was a woman of power who corrupted the true religion in that city. Wesley marks the difference from the previous letter: at Pergamos were many followers of Balaam and here one grand deceiver, and there they were enticed first to idolatry and then to fornication, here the order reversed. Of the space allowed, Clarke traces the delay to Ahab, whose tokens of repentance put off his punishment and with it hers; Ellicott insists the Greek is to repent out of, so true repentance forsakes the sin; and Wesley draws the conclusion the others leave implicit, that though repentance is God's gift, man may refuse it, and God will not compel.
22:
The bed they all read as retaliation in kind, and Ellicott puts it shortest: the chamber of voluptuousness will become the chamber of sickness, and the spot of the sin shall be the scene of the punishment. Barnes says it is not a bed of ease but of pain, the harlot's bed and the sick bed being brought together as they often are in providence, since the one cannot be indulged without leading sooner or later to the sufferings of the other. Robertson borrows Beckwith's phrase, a bed of sickness against the bed of adultery, and notes the present tense is used rather than the future because judgment is imminent. Clarke traces the figure to Ahaziah, son of Ahab and Jezebel, who followed his mother's ways and was punished by a fall from the terrace over his house, lying bedridden long in great anguish so that he might have room to repent; and when instead he sent to consult Baalzebub, Elijah pronounced a final doom.

Whether her children are her own or her followers nobody will decide. Barnes says the word admits either interpretation and nothing in the connection determines it. Robertson offers the same alternative, either her actual children, after the fate of Ahab's sons, or, in Swete's phrase, her spiritual progeny who have accepted her practices. Ellicott takes them for her followers and marks the progression: the so-called prophetess led the way in looseness of morals under pretence of deeper knowledge, she had her associates and their disciples, and the disciples outrun their teachers, so that more than tribulation is their penalty. Clarke keeps to the history, where Jezebel's two sons, both kings, were slain, and after them the seventy sons of Ahab. Wesley reads the killing as death by plague or some manifest stroke, and thinks the vengeance on her children the token of the certainty of all the rest.

The depths of Satan Ellicott takes as a phrase the teachers themselves used. Like the Gnostics after them they professed a deeper insight into the deep things of God, and may have garnished their speech with this very phrase, borrowed in sound though not in sense from the Corinthians, and may even have boasted of their knowledge of Satan; but such knowledge, he says, was purchased too dearly. Wesley exclaims over it: happy ignorance, and our Lord owns the things were deep, deep as hell, being the very depths of Satan; then he asks whether these were the depths of which Luther speaks, adding that it is well if there are not some of Luther's countrymen now in England who know them too well. Robertson notes that those who held out were not necessarily a minority, and that the verb means they did not come to know by experience.

The rod of iron and the morning star Clarke and Robertson take in opposite directions. Clarke reads both politically: the rod restrains vice by the strictest administration of justice, and seems to refer to the heathen world, perhaps to Constantine, who in overcoming Licinius became the instrument of destroying idolatry over the Roman empire, so that it was broken like fragments of an earthen vessel; and since sun, moon and stars are emblems of empires, the morning star means the brightest empire next to Christ's own. Robertson refuses the transfer: in the last chapter Christ is himself the bright morning star, so that the victor will have Christ himself. Wesley turns the promise into a prayer, that Jesus is the morning star and should give himself, after which one desires no sun but him who is also the sun, for he whom this star enlightens has always morning and no evening. Ellicott calls it the pledge of the coming day; Barnes describes the planet itself, intermingled with the first rays of the sun; and Gill sees in it the Reformation, the twilight before the day.
